1.pericope_label: And the rulers of the people dwelt at Jerusalem: the rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts to dwell in other cities. And the people blessed all the men, that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem.

schools.summary: Delitzsch identifies the province of the heading as the land of Judah under Persian administration and warns against reading a contrast into the repeated verb about dwelling, which is a mere pleonasm.

Gill gives the practical grounds for the rulers living in the capital — their offices, its defence, and the example that would encourage others — and distinguishes the volunteers from those the lot had taken, noting that the people wished them happiness because they had given up ease and profit for the common good.

Clarke calls the voluntary offer a sacrifice to patriotism, the city affording few advantages and considerable danger; Wesley puts it harder still, that Jerusalem was the butt of every malicious plot and for the present cost its inhabitants more than it brought them.

Henry asks why the holy city had to be repopulated by lot at all and gives three reasons for the reluctance: a stricter manner of life was expected there, it was the place most hated by the surrounding nations, and it was simply poorer than the farming country; he turns the third into a general complaint that most people prefer their own wealth, credit, ease and safety to the glory of God, and observes of the rulers that the mighty are magnetic, their example bringing holiness into reputation.

themes: And the rulers of the people dwelt at Jerusalem: the rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts to dwell in other cities.
And the people blessed all the men, that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem.

3.pericope_label: Now these are the chief of the province that dwelt in Jerusalem: but in the cities of Judah dwelt every one in his possession in their cities, to wit, Israel, the priests, and the Levites, and the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon’s servants. And at Jerusalem dwelt certain of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin. Of the children of Judah; Athaiah the son of Uzziah, the son of Zechariah, the son of Amariah, the son of Shephatiah, the son of Mahalaleel, of the children of Perez; And Maaseiah the son of Baruch, the son of Col–hozeh, the son of Hazaiah, the son of Adaiah, the son of Joiarib, the son of Zechariah, the son of Shiloni.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the writer's own position in the word province, betraying a man who was a Persian official as well as governor of Judah, and treats the sentence as a general heading covering country as well as capital, with Israel used generically; Delitzsch sorts the Judahite entries into two heads from the lines of Perez and Shelah, repeats his correction of the pointing of the second name, and counts the total as heads of families rather than individuals.

Gill glosses the province as Judea, reduced by Babylon and now held under Persia, makes Jerusalem's double tribal population a consequence of its straddling the boundary of Judah and Benjamin, and works the second Judahite pedigree back to a forefather he suspects is Shelah under another form.

Clarke finds a real difference of scope between this register and the parallel, that one numbering only those who returned with Zerubbabel while this adds the people who came up later with Ezra and with Nehemiah; Wesley glosses the province and reads Israel as the generality of the people.

themes: Now these are the chief of the province that dwelt in Jerusalem: but in the cities of Judah dwelt every one in his possession in their cities, to wit, Israel, the priests, and the Levites, and the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon’s servants.

And at Jerusalem dwelt certain of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin. Of the children of Judah; Athaiah the son of Uzziah, the son of Zechariah, the son of Amariah, the son of Shephatiah, the son of Mahalaleel, of the children of Perez;
And Maaseiah the son of Baruch, the son of Col–hozeh, the son of Hazaiah, the son of Adaiah, the son of Joiarib, the son of Zechariah, the son of Shiloni.

6.pericope_label: All the sons of Perez that dwelt at Jerusalem were four hundred threescore and eight valiant men. And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jesaiah. And after him Gabbai, Sallai, nine hundred twenty and eight. And Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer: and Judah the son of Senuah was second over the city. Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin.

schools.summary: Delitzsch counts two Benjamite heads rather than three, reading the second name as a single compound, and takes the totals as fathers of families; on the priests he explains that the word for son crept in before one name by a copyist's slip, identifies the ruler of the house of God as a descendant of Ahitub, and numbers the ministering priests of the three orders; Ellicott likewise reads the opening priestly names as three families and counts the two Benjamite houses that supplied the city's two prefects.

Gill reads the description of the Judahite men as bearing on why they were wanted, valiant men qualified to defend the city, notices that Benjamin supplied more men than Judah and offers two explanations, and records that the priestly account matches the parallel except for one name given in another form.

Clarke makes the first named officer magistrate and the second his deputy, while allowing that they may have held different offices rather than one office at two levels; Wesley gives the first a military sense, as captain of their thousand.

debates.question: How many men stand behind the second Benjamite name?

positions.position: Two — Gabbai and Sallai, following the head of the house.
One, a single compound name, giving Benjamin two heads rather than three.

themes: All the sons of Perez that dwelt at Jerusalem were four hundred threescore and eight valiant men.
And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jesaiah.
And after him Gabbai, Sallai, nine hundred twenty and eight.
And Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer: and Judah the son of Senuah was second over the city.
Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin.

11.pericope_label: Seraiah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, was the ruler of the house of God. And their brethren that did the work of the house were eight hundred twenty and two: and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pelaliah, the son of Amzi, the son of Zechariah, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchiah, And his brethren, chief of the fathers, two hundred forty and two: and Amashai the son of Azareel, the son of Ahasai, the son of Meshillemoth, the son of Immer, And their brethren, mighty men of valour, an hundred twenty and eight: and their overseer was Zabdiel, the son of one of the great men. Also of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hashub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Bunni;

schools.summary: Delitzsch runs the ruler's pedigree back through Hilkiah and Zadok to Ahitub, sets out the three totals as heads of families, and names the overseer of the last group; Ellicott refuses the martial reading of the phrase about valour, glossing it as ability for the service of God's house, and corrects the description of the overseer's father into a proper name.

Gill explains what the largest priestly figure covers — the men who offered the sacrifices, burnt the incense, set on the shewbread and lit the lamps — identifies the second company as kinsmen of the head just named, and takes the description of the third both ways, as able men for priestly office and as men who could fight if occasion arose.
Clarke reads the same phrase as plainly military, marking the men for strength of body and courage in war.

debates.question: What does mighty men of valour mean here?

positions.position: Both at once — capable in priestly office and able to defend the city.
Military: strength of body and courage in war.
Not martial at all — ability for the service of God’s house.

themes: Seraiah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, was the ruler of the house of God.

And their brethren that did the work of the house were eight hundred twenty and two: and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pelaliah, the son of Amzi, the son of Zechariah, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchiah,
And his brethren, chief of the fathers, two hundred forty and two: and Amashai the son of Azareel, the son of Ahasai, the son of Meshillemoth, the son of Immer,
And their brethren, mighty men of valour, an hundred twenty and eight: and their overseer was Zabdiel, the son of one of the great men.

16.pericope_label: And Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chief of the Levites, had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God. And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer: and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun. All the Levites in the holy city were two hundred fourscore and four. Moreover the porters, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two.

schools.summary: Delitzsch distinguishes the outward business of the house from the service within it and gives the musical office as the principal to begin the thanksgiving, with a second standing next among his brethren; Ellicott stops on the gatekeepers' figure because the parallel gives a larger one, and offers a partial explanation only — that the other list is confined to those who returned with Zerubbabel while this adds the men who came with Ezra.

Gill sets the two officers of the outward business alongside the Levite named before them, notes that one forefather in the musical pedigree appears under another form in the parallel record, and gives the totals of Levites and gatekeepers as the verse has them.

Clarke translates the musical office into his own vocabulary as precentor, pitcher of the tune, master-singer; Wesley describes the occasion instead, the public prayers and praises joined constantly to the morning and evening sacrifice, at which the singers were present and praised God with a psalm this man began.

themes: And Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chief of the Levites, had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God.

And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer: and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun.

20.pericope_label: And the residue of Israel, of the priests, and the Levites, were in all the cities of Judah, every one in his inheritance. But the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel: and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims.

schools.summary: Delitzsch places Ophel on the southern slope of Mount Moriah, names the two chiefs set over the temple servants, and declines another scholar's identification of one of them with a name in the earlier roll, since descent from a man is no reason to suppose a chief was that man; Ellicott raises and leaves open whether the promontory counted as inside the city, judging that here it is treated as outside.
Gill states the fact plainly, that the rest of Israel with its priests and Levites lived outside the city, every man in his own inheritance, and describes Ophel as a high point or tower on the wall.
Wesley gives the same location on the wall and the same reason for it.

Henry warns against the quarrel the arrangement might produce — no strife, no envy, no contempt between the people of the cities and those of the villages, since the king himself is served by the field and both are needful — and explains the settling of the temple servants against the wall by the servile work of the temple falling to them, which required them near at hand.

themes: And the residue of Israel, of the priests, and the Levites, were in all the cities of Judah, every one in his inheritance.
But the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel: and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims.

22.pericope_label: The overseer also of the Levites at Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Micha. Of the sons of Asaph, the singers were over the business of the house of God. For it was the king’s commandment concerning them, that a certain portion should be for the singers, due for every day. And Pethahiah the son of Meshezabeel, of the children of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king’s hand in all matters concerning the people.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the verse as repairing an omission, the chief of one Levitical division having been left unnamed earlier because he was over the singers, who had not then been mentioned, and he holds that the officer at the king's hand can scarcely be a commissioner stationed in Jerusalem but a man transacting the community's affairs at the king's court; Ellicott calls him instead the king's agent in the country business of the province, and observes that this man's descent from Zerah makes the absence of Zerah from the tribal lists at the head of the chapter very remarkable.

Gill describes the overseer as the man who saw that the Levites did their work in ministering to the priests, traces his descent to Asaph, and on the question of which king provided for the singers reports the two opinions before preferring the king of Persia.

Clarke renders the overseer's title as visitant or inspector, judges the providing king to be the Persian rather than David, and places the royal agent in Judah as governor over the nation in matters where the civil power touched Jewish concerns, supposing he fixed and levied the tribute; Wesley describes that work as judging civil causes by the law of that kingdom, between man and man and between the king and the people.

Henry notes what kept a scattered order together, an overseer resident in the capital to whom they applied for direction and who took cognisance of their conduct, and adds that some of the singers were set to look after the temple's repairs between services, being ingenious men with time on their hands.

debates.question: Where did the officer at the king's hand sit?

positions.position: At the king's court, transacting the community's affairs there.
In Judah, as the royal agent over the province and its tribute.

themes: The overseer also of the Levites at Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Micha. Of the sons of Asaph, the singers were over the business of the house of God.
For it was the king’s commandment concerning them, that a certain portion should be for the singers, due for every day.
And Pethahiah the son of Meshezabeel, of the children of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king’s hand in all matters concerning the people.

25.pericope_label: And for the villages, with their fields, some of the children of Judah dwelt at Kirjath–arba, and in the villages thereof, and at Dibon, and in the villages thereof, and at Jekabzeel, and in the villages thereof, And at Jeshua, and at Moladah, and at Beth–phelet,

schools.summary: Delitzsch describes the change of unit — the heads of houses outside Jerusalem are no longer enumerated, only the towns with their attached settlements, and even those summarily — notes the particle introducing the section as peculiar to this passage, glosses the word for villages as properly meaning enclosures, and reads the closing summary as a statement of how much ground the tribe was holding again.
Gill marks the transition to the country cities and villages and lets the place-names carry their own weight without pressing them for more than they say.

themes: And for the villages, with their fields, some of the children of Judah dwelt at Kirjath–arba, and in the villages thereof, and at Dibon, and in the villages thereof, and at Jekabzeel, and in the villages thereof,
And at Jeshua, and at Moladah, and at Beth–phelet,

30.pericope_label: Zanoah, Adullam, and in their villages, at Lachish, and the fields thereof, at Azekah, and in the villages thereof. And they dwelt from Beer–sheba unto the valley of Hinnom. The children also of Benjamin from Geba dwelt at Michmash, and Aija, and Beth–el, and in their villages, And at Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah, Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim,

schools.summary: Ellicott measures the southern reach at some fifty miles, the extreme south to the extreme north of Judah, and would render the Benjamite clause so that the tribe is said to have dwelt from Geba onward; Delitzsch places Geba as the northern boundary of the kingdom of Judah at a half-ruined village three leagues north of Jerusalem, equates Michmash with a site still bearing a form of the name, and reads the closing note about the Levites as recording a movement of divisions from Judah into Benjamin rather than a boundary.

Gill places Geba on the southern border of Benjamin and Michmash on the northern so that the two bracket the tribe's land, and works through the remaining names as a gazetteer, identifying what he can and admitting that two are mentioned nowhere else.
Clarke suggests Geba is probably the Gibeah associated with Saul, and calls two of the towns Gill identifies simply unknown.

positions.position: On the southern border of Benjamin, bracketing the tribe's land with Michmash.
The northern boundary of the kingdom of Judah, three leagues north of Jerusalem.
Probably the same place as the Gibeah associated with Saul.

themes: Zanoah, Adullam, and in their villages, at Lachish, and the fields thereof, at Azekah, and in the villages thereof. And they dwelt from Beer–sheba unto the valley of Hinnom.

35.pericope_label: Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen. And of the Levites were divisions in Judah, and in Benjamin.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the brevity of the notice by the fewness of the Levites in the country.
Gill takes the divisions to mean the Levites were scattered through both tribes, and gives the reason he thinks governed it — the better instruction of the people.

Clarke reports that the last pair of towns were raised by the sons of a man recorded in the Benjamite genealogies, suspects the valley of craftsmen was a trade quarter built in the valley that named it, rejects the ancient version that would give the Levites half of each tribe, and observes that however willing the people now were, their provision for the ministry cannot have been great while the full service was unestablished and the Levites few.

themes: Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen.
And of the Levites were divisions in Judah, and in Benjamin.
